# Compacted Summary: Chapter 1 (Complete and Final – Updated 50)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August, then Christmas/New Year period of first year; now nearly three weeks into new year (1832); just after Lords threw out the Reform Bill
- **Primary Location**: Middlemarch and surrounding areas (Lowick, the Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Wilhaven, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Salmere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring)
- **Atmospheric Details**: Baker's boy frequently late; wind off water with salt and tar smell; dog barking periodically; bees in lavender behind parsonage; gulls quarreling over fish heads; frost silvering hedges; road rutted and puddled after thaw; children chasing hoops down lane; light going early; chalk sun on forge wall; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; turnip carts passing; bell for vespers ringing thinly; rain threatening since morning but holding off; sky heavy

## Main Characters

**Dorothea**
- Recently widowed; residing at Lowick Manor
- **Financial Status**: Has seven hundred a-year of her own fortune, nineteen hundred a-year from Casaubon, and between three and four thousand of ready money in the bank; has dislike to Casaubon's property
- **Conviction About Lydgate**: Feels convinced Lydgate's conduct not guilty
- **Plan to Help Lydgate**: Wrote brief note enclosing check for a thousand pounds
- **Devastating Discovery at Lydgate's House**: Heard voice speaking in low tones; saw Will Ladislaw seated on sofa with Rosamond close by, flushed and tearful, Will clasping both her upraised hands in his, speaking with low-toned fervor; in terrible illumination of certainty, paused motionless, laid down letter on small table, went quickly out
- **Night of Anguish**: Experienced waves of suffering shaking her thoroughly; cried in loud whispers between sobs after her lost belief in Will and lost joy of silent love; lay on bare floor as night grew cold; saw two images—Rosamond and Will—tearing her heart as if divided by sword
- **Morning Awakening**: Awoke in chill hours with clearest consciousness of looking into eyes of sorrow; wrapped warm things around her; seated herself in great chair; soul liberated from terrible conflict; no longer wrestling with grief but could sit with it as lasting companion
- **Second Visit to Lydgate's House**: Came to speak about injustice shown towards Lydgate; spoke quite simply, gathering firmness as she went on; emphasized Lydgate feels his life bound into one with Rosamond's; experienced emotional breaking point; when Rosamond, taken hold of by emotion stronger than her own, hurried along in new movement, the two women clasped each other as if they had been in a shipwreck
- **Revelation from Rosamond**: Rosamond disclosed that Will loves another woman (Dorothea), said Will claims no other woman existed for him beside Dorothea, said blame is entirely hers, said he could never explain to Dorothea because of her, but said she has now told Dorothea
- **Revulsion of Feeling**: Revulsion of feeling too strong to be called joy; tumult in which terrible strain of night and morning made resistant pain; immediate consciousness one of immense sympathy without check; cared for Rosamond without struggle now
- **Evening Encounter with Will in Library**: Could not receive him in library where husband's prohibition seemed to dwell; when door opened and she saw Will, she did not move; he came towards her with more doubt and timidity than she had ever seen before, afraid lest some look or word condemn him to new distance; Dorothea afraid of her own emotion; looked as if spell upon her kept her motionless, hindering her from unclasping her hands
- **Will's Explanation**: Will explained affair now matter of gossip; something connected with it helped bring him down here again—idea of getting Bulstrode to apply money to public purpose, money Bulstrode had thought of giving him; Bulstrode privately offered compensation for old injury and good income to make amends; told her if it were new hardship it would be new reason for him to cling to her, nothing could have changed him but thinking she was different, not so good as he had believed; said she would believe him better than he is in everything but one—his truth to her
- **Storm Scene and Hand-Clasping**: Stood with Will silent not looking at each other but at evergreens being tossed showing pale underside of leaves against blackening sky; lightning made them start and look at each other and smile; when vivid flash of lightning lit each of them for the other, Dorothea darted instantaneously from window; Will followed, seizing her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children looking out on storm; thunder gave tremendous crack and roll; rain began to pour down; turned faces towards each other with memory of his last words in them; did not loose each other's hands
- **Will's Despairing Words**: Will said there is no hope for him, even if she loved him as well as he loves her, even if he were everything to her, he shall most likely always be very poor, on sober calculation one can count on nothing but creeping lot, impossible for them ever to belong to each other, perhaps base of him to have asked for word from her, he meant to go away into silence but has not been able to do what he meant
- **Will's Continued Bitterness**: Will said it is cruel of Dorothea to speak in that way—as if there were any comfort, she may see beyond the misery of it, but he doesn't, it is unkind—it is throwing back his love for her as if it were a trifle, they can never be married; expressed that it is a mere toss up whether he shall ever do more than keep himself decently, unless he chooses to sell himself as a mere pen and a mouthpiece, could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce
- **Heart Full of Words**: Her heart was full of something she wanted to say, and yet the words were too difficult; she was wholly possessed by them: at that moment debate was mute within her; it was very hard that she could not say what she wanted to say
- **Will's Departure and Her Response**: Will looked out of the window angrily; if he would have looked at her and not gone away from her side, she thought everything would have been easier; at last he turned, still resting against the chair, and stretching his hand automatically towards his hat, said with a sort of exasperation, "Good-by"; in an instant she spoke; Will was close to her and had his arms round her, but she drew her head back and held his away gently that she might go on speaking, her large tear-filled eyes looking at his very simply, while she said in a sobbing childlike way, "We could live quite well on my own fortune—it is too much—seven hundred a-year—I want so little—no new clothes—and I will learn what everything costs"
- **Engagement and Plans**: Has sent for her uncle Mr. Brooke to Lowick; the matter came about quite suddenly—neither Will nor Dorothea had any idea two days ago; Dorothea is quite determined to act as she likes; Mr. Brooke will give her away but plans to cut off the entail (will cost money and be troublesome)
- **Celia's Visit to Lowick**: Celia traveled to Lowick to influence Dorothea's mind; through their girlhood felt she could act on her sister by a word judiciously placed; as matron feels more able to advise her childless sister; expressed shock at Dorothea's decision, said she has disappointed them all, that it is very bad, questioned how Dorothea can marry Ladislaw with no estate, noted how it shocks James dreadfully, called it all so different from what Dorothea has always been; referenced Dorothea's former reasons for marrying Casaubon (his great soul, learning, age, dismalness) and expressed bewilderment at her marrying Ladislaw instead

**Will Ladislaw**
- Passionate love for Dorothea
- **Public Scandal**: Genealogy now public knowledge via Bambridge's disclosure; described as having "queer genealogy"—high-spirited young lady, musical Polish patriot, with "grafting of the Jew pawnbroker"
- **Scene at Lydgate's House**: Seated with Rosamond on sofa, clasping both her upraised hands, speaking with low-toned fervor; when Rosamond became aware of Dorothea's presence and snatched away her hands, Will looked round also; meeting Dorothea's eyes with new lightning in them, seemed changing to marble
- **Anguish After Dorothea's Departure**: Stood motionless with Rosamond; looked towards spot where Dorothea stood; said sharply "Don't touch me!" with utterance like cut of lash; darted from Rosamond; wheeled round to other side of room with tips of fingers in pockets and head thrown back, looking fiercely; expressed inability to explain his passion and that no other woman existed for him beside Dorothea
- **Plans to Return to Middlemarch**: As exile, had placed no stronger obstacle to his return than his own resolve—not iron barrier but state of mind liable to melt; as months went on, seemed more difficult to say why he should not run down merely to hear something about Dorothea; hunger had tamed him and he became very hungry for vision of certain form and sound of certain voice; took Riverston coach and came back again; made up mind he must go to Lydgate's that evening
- **Visit to Lydgate's House**: Received by Rosamond with languid coldness; Rosamond sat in silence bending over work; when Rosamond poured tea, she placed tiny bit of folded paper in his saucer; he secured it quickly; opened and read it by bed-candle; effect made cheeks and ears burn thinking of what occurred between Dorothea and Rosamond; felt uncertainty how far Dorothea might still feel dignity wounded; feared lasting flaw in her mind
- **Evening in Library with Dorothea**: Came towards her with more doubt and timidity than she had ever seen before, afraid lest some look or word condemn him to new distance; took her hand and raised it to his lips with something like a sob; stood with hat and gloves in other hand; difficult to loose hand; felt very happy leaning on chair, not much afraid of anything she might feel; stood silent not looking at each other but at evergreens being tossed showing pale underside of leaves; lightning made them start and look at each other and smile; when vivid flash of lightning lit each of them for the other, seized her hand with spasmodic movement; they stood with hands clasped like two children looking out on storm; turned faces towards each other; did not loose each other's hands
- **Expressions of Despair and Love**: Said it must be that they can never be married, it is cruel of her to speak in that way—as if there were any comfort, it is unkind—it is throwing back his love for her as if it were a trifle; expressed that it is a mere toss up whether he shall ever do more than keep himself decently, unless he chooses to sell himself as a mere pen and a mouthpiece, could not offer himself to any woman, even if she had no luxuries to renounce; looked out of the window angrily; at last he turned, still resting against the chair, and stretching his hand automatically towards his hat, said with a sort of exasperation, "Good-by"
- **Reversal When Dorothea Speaks**: When she spoke in a sobbing childlike way about living quite well on her own fortune of seven hundred a-year, wanting so little, no new clothes, willing to learn what everything costs, Will was close to her and had his arms round her
- **Engagement**: Is now engaged to marry Dorothea; has "objectionable position" and "bad origin" per Sir James

**Lydgate**
- **Moral Crisis**: Constructed probabilities case—Bulstrode feared scandalous disclosures from Raffles; may have tampered with patient or disobeyed orders; acknowledges "just possible" sometimes true; questions whether he would have acted identically without money
- **Social Ostracism**: Patients avoiding him; practice and reputation utterly damned; general black-balling begun
- **Interview with Dorothea**: Told her everything from first application to Bulstrode under pressure of difficulties; disclosed his doubts and uneasy consciousness that accepting money made some difference in private inclination; wrote letter of gratitude
- **Final Resolution**: Declines continuing at Hospital; must get away from Middlemarch as soon as possible
- **Evening with Will**: Will arrived looking rather battered; felt inexpressibly mournful when discussing settling in London
- **Return Home and Rosamond's Illness**: Found Rosamond ill on bed, soothed and tended her for next hour
- **Morning After**: Saw Dorothea's letter on drawing-room table with check for a thousand pounds; Rosamond made no reply when he mentioned Ladislaw sat with him last night
- **Second Visit from Dorothea**: Led Dorothea to drawing-room, put his letter of gratitude into her hands, then went upstairs; told Rosamond gently that Mrs. Casaubon had come to see her again; when he returned after going to Coleman's, noticed both women needed care; offered to order Dorothea's carriage
- **Evening Scene**: Has accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation; chosen fragile Rosamond and taken burden of her life upon his arms; must walk carrying that burden pitifully; felt thankful when Rosamond showed little mark of interest in him, pushing back his hair; prepared Rosamond's room for evening; when Will visited evening and Rosamond poured tea, Lydgate innocently remained in room and noticed nothing amiss; apologized indirectly for Rosamond's exhaustion by suggesting she rest

**Rosamond Lydgate**
- Married to Lydgate; victorious obstinacy never wasting energy
- **Crisis Response**: When scandal broke, shock was terrible; felt shame was worst part of crime
- **Before Scene at Home**: Regained brilliant health; determined to tell Will Ladislaw everything when he comes; morning descended equipped for walk with letter to Mr. Ladislaw written with charming discretion
- **Scene with Will**: With bonnet hanging back, sat flushed and tearful, turned towards Will who leaned towards her clasping both her upraised hands; when Dorothea entered, snatched away her hands and rose; under first great shock that shattered her dream-world; strange unexpected manifestation of Dorothea's feeling made her soul totter
- **Will's Anger**: Had no sense of chill resolute repulsion such as known under Lydgate's displeasure; all her sensibility turned into bewildering novelty of pain; felt new terrified recoil under lash never experienced before; became image of sickened misery with pale lips and eyes with tearless dismay
- **Morning After**: Sat languidly wondering what to do next; looked ill but recovered her usual quietude; Rosamond made no reply when Lydgate told her of Dorothea's letter with check and that Ladislaw sat with him
- **Response to Dorothea's Second Visit**: Colored and gave startled movement when Lydgate said Mrs. Casaubon come to see her again; did not say no despite daring not touch yesterday's facts; Will's lacerating words made every thought of Dorothea fresh smart; in humiliating uncertainty dared do nothing but comply; pride broken down between the two women; disclosed to Dorothea that Will loves another woman (Dorothea), told her she has told Dorothea and he cannot reproach her anymore; asked "Tertius did not find fault with me, then?" understanding that Lydgate might have said anything to Mrs. Casaubon; smile began to play over Dorothea's face; poor Rosamond's vagrant fancy come back terribly scourged—meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; shelter was still there; her husband had accepted his narrowed lot with sad resignation
- **This Evening**: Prepared for Will's visit; received him with languid coldness; sat in silence bending over bit of work; when poured tea and Will came near to fetch it, placed tiny bit of folded paper in his saucer; had written note to him with neatly flowing hand (content unspecified)

## Family Reactions to Engagement

**Sir James Chettam**
- **Response to News**: Still in white indignation; said if Ladislaw had spark of honor he would have gone out of country at once and never shown his face in it again; said he was not surprised, the day after Casaubon's funeral he said what ought to be done but was not listened to; unable to repress retort saying high opinion of Ladislaw by Brooke led to his lodging in neighborhood; called it perfectly scandalous, saying Dorothea degrading herself by marrying him; emphasized delicacy ought to have forbidden her seeing him again after husband's will; listed grievances: Ladislaw takes her from proper rank into poverty, has meanness to accept such sacrifice, always had objectionable position, bad origin, man of little principle and light character; said he himself cannot take Ladislaw into family and must speak for himself; acknowledged to himself (though ashamed of it) that part of his opposition stems from jealous repugnance not entirely different from his reaction to Casaubon; acknowledges marriage fatal for Dorothea; also motivated by undeniable fact that union of two estates—Tipton and Freshitt—lying charmingly within ring-fence was prospect that flattered him for his son and heir; when Mr. Brooke mentioned cutting off entail, Sir James felt sudden embarrassment, stoppage in throat, blushed; found more words than usual in first jet of anger, but Mr. Brooke's propitiation more clogging to his tongue than Mr. Cadwallader's caustic hint

**Mr. Brooke** (Dorothea's uncle)
- **Previous Conversation with Dorothea**: Tried to dissuade her, pointed out poverty and abandoning her position, said "My dear, you don't know what it is to live on seven hundred a-year, and have no carriage, and that kind of thing, and go amongst people who don't know who you are"; spoke strongly to her but she quite determined to act as she likes
- **Family Discussion**: Looking dejected at Freshitt Hall, came forward with evident nervous perturbation; told family about Dorothea—went to Lowick after she sent for him; it had come about quite suddenly—neither Will nor Dorothea had any idea two days ago; he put it strongly to her, did his duty, but she can act as she likes; advised Sir James to talk to Dorothea herself; mentioned fact that she has dislike to Casaubon's property
- **Financial Plan**: Can cut off the entail; will cost money and be troublesome; he showed his own force of resolution and propitiated what was just in Baronet's vexation; touched a motive of which Sir James was ashamed

**Mr. Cadwallader** (the Rector)
- **Defense of Dorothea**: Said to be just to Chettam; objected to all unnecessary discomfort; acknowledged Mrs. Casaubon may be acting imprudently, giving up fortune for man, but said should not condemn as wrong action in strict sense because men have such poor opinion of each other; said they are rather apt to consider act wrong because it is unpleasant to them; like many men who take life easily, had knack of saying home truth occasionally to those who felt themselves virtuously out of temper; said should not make any fuss about it, if she likes to be poor that is her affair; said nobody would have said anything if she had married young fellow because he was rich; noted plenty of beneficed clergy are poorer than they will be; referenced his own case: had hardly thousand a-year, was lout, nobody could see anything in him, shoes were not right cut, all men wondered how woman could like him; said must take Ladislaw's part until hearing more harm of him

**Mrs. Cadwallader**
- **Pointed Remarks**: Noted "there is usually a silent exception in such cases"; said only wonder to her is that any of them are surprised; blamed them for doing nothing to hinder it; said if they had had Lord Triton down here to woo her with his philanthropy, he might have carried her off before year was over; said "There was no safety in anything else"; blamed Mr. Casaubon for preparing it all beautifully by making himself disagreeable or it pleasing God to make him so, then daring her to contradict him; said it is way to make any trumpery tempting, to ticket it at high price in that way

**Celia Chettam**
- Thought it would be of great use to take journey to Lowick to influence Dorothea's mind; through girlhood felt she could act on her sister by word judiciously placed by opening little window for daylight of her own understanding to enter among strange colored lamps by which Dodo habitually saw; as matron naturally felt more able to advise her childless sister
- **At Lowick**: Said to Dorothea in her placid guttural: it is very bad, you have disappointed us all so; expressed disbelief that marriage "ever will be"—Dorothea never can go live in that way; referenced all her plans; noted James would have taken any trouble for her and she might have gone on all her life doing what she liked; noted Dorothea always wanted things that wouldn't do, but other plans would have come; expressed shock: "how can you marry Mr. Ladislaw, that we none of us ever thought you could marry? It shocks James so dreadfully. And then it is all so different from what you have always been. You would have Mr. Casaubon because he had such a great soul, and was so old and dismal and learned; and now, to think of marrying Mr. Ladislaw, who has got no estate or anything. I suppose it is because you must be making yourself uncomfortable in some way or other."

## Incidental Details - Rumors/Unverified Claims
- Only Cotho Hollwood knew that the Lindson family once owed a blood debt to the Hollmere family
- Only Breena Orlwood knew that the Lindson mill ledger was rewritten after the flood
- Only Cotho Hollwood knew that the fire at the Salford granary was set on purpose
- Only Breena Orlwood knew that the old abbey at Salford hides a second cellar
- Only Nynelle Stenworth knew that the deed to the Bryngate pastures was forged
- Only Feten Lindner knew that a chest of silver lies buried beneath the well at Mirecombe
- Only Thiena Hollwood alone carried the knowledge that the bridge toll at Salwick is skimmed every month
- It was an old law of Quenwick that the vault beneath its chapel would open only for a living person who held both the jade ring and the oak comb at once
- The toll bridge at Dunholt belonged to the Wexwood family, and only those born a Wexwood, or presently married to one, were allowed to cross it

## Artifacts
- The jade ring belonged to Orvie Hollett
- Brevie Hollmere kept the amber mirror in a cedar box
- The jade chalice belonged to Islan Lindner, head of the Lindner household; by custom always passes on death of holder to eldest living child of that holder; no will could change this; it passed without ceremony
- The tortoise-shell lozenge-box: seen by Dorothea in Miss Noble's basket; color mounted to Dorothea's cheeks upon seeing it
